entries.title: White Sox' Will Venable named AL Manager of the Year
entries.summary: <p>When the nine-year MLB playing career that he’s always underselling ended,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> manager Will Venable started out with the amorphous job title that’s often the stuff of envy across the industry: <i>special assistant</i>.</p><p>What he found about himself eventually landed him in a position on the opposite side of the spectrum for public scrutiny.</p><p>“I like to help players be better,” Venable told the Sun-Times in September, when asked what part of his job doesn’t feel like work. “They each require a certain type of attention and support that we have to figure out. I like to figure out that puzzle, and I also really enjoy just being responsible for the overall environment.”</p><p>After 84 wins, the franchise’s first playoff series victory in 21 years, and a summer where the White Sox’ environment was the envy of the league, Venable is the American League Manager of the Year in his second season. He appeared on 29 of 30 ballots and received 15 first-place votes to edge out Kevin Cash, the manager of the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/mlb/2026/11/10/brewers-pat-murphy-first-to-win-three-consecutive-manager-of-year-awards" >Brewers’ Pat Murphy first to win three consecutive Manager of Year awards</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/10/white-sox-remain-set-on-adding-impact-starting-pitching-even-after-shifting-grant-taylor-to-rotation" >White Sox remain set on adding impact starting pitching, even after shifting Grant Taylor to rotation</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“I do view this very much as an organizational award,” Venable said Tuesday night. “Because we are such a collaborative group, really at every level of our organization, starting with ownership.”</p><p>His players would argue there are limits to how much Venable should be allowed to defer credit.</p><p>“Everything starts with Will,” said Miguel Vargas in October, who has gone from fighting for his place in the league to an All-Star over Venable’s tenure. “The way he lets us lead the clubhouse. He’s an example every single day for us too. He lets us be ourselves and have fun.”</p><p>“When you have guys trying to prove themselves to their own dugout or to their own teammates, it’s usually a toxic culture that isn’t going to get you anywhere,” said starting pitcher Davis Martin. “We built something special here where you know good, bad, or indifferent of how you perform on the field, you know the guys love you for who you are.”</p><p>Sometimes, praising Venable’s soft skills can be a way of eliding discussion of in-game tactics, which his team’s success brought under greater scrutiny.</p><p>His style is busy — the Sox led MLB in relief innings, were third in pinch-hitters, fourth in pinch-runners — offering countless points for second-guessing. Talking to Venable reveals his moves to be resting upon a latticework of research from analysts, workload restrictions from medical staff, and other considerations invisible to the public, rather than easily defended baseball bromides.</p><p>While Venable is process-oriented to a degree that’s unfamiliar to this franchise, he wears the moves that don’t work in the traditional fashion.</p><p>“Perfection is impossible, but he’s always trying to be [perfect], and that’s what the great ones do,” said Sox field coordinator, and Venable’s close friend Chris Denorfia, who joined the coaching staff this year. “I knew that he was good at this. But I am almost in a constant sense of awe and amazement just watching him.”</p><p>Denorfia talks of a “million little processes” Venable puts his staff through in the name of constantly improving the White Sox operation, of which their award-winning skipper now seems like an essential part. The team rarely discusses contract details of staff members publicly, and the sixth manager of the year award in franchise history has yet to make the Sox start talking about an extension for Venable.</p><p>Still, their feelings are pretty clear.</p><p>“He’s been a tremendous partner,” said general manager Chris Getz. “My hope is that Will and I can work together for a long time.”</p><p></p><h3>Vote total (Tabulated on a 5-3-1 basis)</h3><h3></h3><table id="rte-6893ac20-dd70-11f1-a473-d15e8106e038"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">1st place </td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">2nd place</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">3rd place</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">Total</td></tr><tr style="box-sizing: border-box; entries.title: The Bears have problems, but are they as dramatic as those of the other presumed Super Bowl contenders?
entries.summary: <p>Three things I think I know about the 7-2 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, who — “a win is a win” baloney aside — backed into a bye week with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/08/bears-grades-buccaneers-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-chicago-sunday-night-soldier-field-nfl" target="_blank" >mistake-filled 27-24 near-disaster against the Buccaneers</a> at Soldier Field:</p><p><b>1. At least they have first-world problems: </b>Heading into Tuesday’s trade deadline, the Bears had a dearth of warm, healthy bodies in their defensive backfield. Their esteemed rushing attack is in a five-game relative lull, all without Kyle Monangai, as D’Andre Swift keeps taking hits. And then there’s the Caleb Williams question: Was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-qb-caleb-williams-must-use-4-interception-game-vs-buccaneers-to-to-keep-growing" target="_blank" >an out-of-nowhere four-interception fiasco</a> just a meaningless one-off or are there cracks in the foundation?</p><p>But look around the league at some of the other leading teams and ask if you’d want the Bears to trade places. The Chiefs, for example, are 6-2, but quarterback Patrick Mahomes hasn’t completed a pass of at least 20 yards through the air since Week 4; thus, the deadline trade for Colts receiver Josh Downs. Beardom would be up for grabs with frustration if Williams were dinking and dunking like the three-time Super Bowl MVP.</p><p>As potent as the 6-3 Packers’ passing game is — and it’s scary-good — they’re still the bottom-ranked rushing team in the NFL, and now they’ll be without Josh Jacobs for another, potentially lengthy stretch. The 6-2 Lions rank 32nd — dead last — against the pass. The 7-1 Bills, commonly viewed as the best team in the NFL, rank 29th against the pass even after winning easily Monday against the Vikings and QB Carson Wentz, who saw Williams’ Sunday-night meltdown and raised him a fat stack of pure incompetence. The Lions and Bills each made a deadline deal for an established DB.</p><p>And the 6-2 Vikings? Before reportedly dealing with the Raiders for old friend Kirk Cousins on Tuesday, they had easily the worst QB1 in the NFC North in Kyler Murray and a reputed QB-whisperer coach, Kevin O’Connell, who couldn’t count on his offense whatsoever. Cousins should be an upgrade, but he’s no Jared Goff, Jordan Love or Williams. This hardly means the Vikings are out of the woods.</p><p>We’re only halfway through the regular season — nine weeks down, nine to go — but some of those flaws were screaming to be addressed. The Bears’ concerns don’t seem as dramatic.</p><p><b>2. Turnovers? What turnovers? </b>After leading the NFL last season in both takeaways and fewest turnovers committed — to the tune of an unreal differential of plus-22 — the Bears have lost their mojo in this area. Their 17 giveaways are tied for third-most in the league. They’re the only team in the division with a negative differential.</p><p>Fudging the numbers sure helps, though. If you take away (get it?) the Bears’ 12 turnovers in their three worst games — five against the Bucs, five against the Packers and two against the Vikings — they’re averaging less than one per outing and are a perfectly wonderful plus-five. See how easy that was?</p><p><b>3. Good, better, give it a rest? </b>Not to tell coach Ben Johnson how to do his job, but he might want to get a new post-win chant warming up in the bullpen. If you watched the video the Bears put out of the locker-room scene Sunday, you might agree the “Good, better, best!” sounded anticlimactic and fell flat. Is a Super Bowl contender going to keep on chanting the same thing, <i>ad infinitum</i>, even after its ugliest of victories? Eventually, there will be a pair of water skis and an Arthur Fonzarelli leather jacket with Johnson’s name on them.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">"Our best football is yet to come" <a href="https://t.co/c3XpbnREtS">pic.twitter.com/c3XpbnREtS</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2119666739889725791?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 9, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Caleb-o-meter: 4 out of 10</b></h3><p>In one impossibly bad quarter, Williams went overboard in paying tribute to Jay Cutler, who rarely was far removed from his last egregious pick thrown while backpedaling.</p><p>Wizardry in the face of pressure, it was not.</p><p>“I’m typically the big eraser,” Williams said.</p><p>If only there were an eraser big enough to wipe this performance from our memories.</p><h3><b>Not halfway bad</b></h3><p><b>The NFL’s top five teams at midseason:</b> 1. Bills, 2. 49ers, 3. Jaguars, 4. Bears, 5. Broncos.</p><p><b>Top five players, offense:</b> 1. Josh Allen, QB, Bills; 2. Joe Burrow, QB, Bengals; 3. Kenneth Walker III, RB, Chiefs; 4. Jordan Love, QB, Packers; 5. Jaxon Smith-Njigba, WR, Seahawks.</p><p><b>Top five players, defense:</b> 1. Will Anderson Jr., DE, Texans; 2. Fred Warner, LB, 49ers; 3. Jeffery Simmons, DT, Bears; 4. Greg Rousseau, LB, Bills; 5. Chase Young, DE, Saints.</p><p><b>Top five coaches: </b>1. John Harbaugh, Giants; 2. Johnson, Bears; 3. Kyle Shanahan, 49ers; 4. Liam Coen, Jaguars; 5. Sean Payton, Broncos.</p><p>You're free to quibble with my selections. I shall allow it this one time only.</p><h3><b>Department of redundancy department</b></h3><p>Even after the Vikings’ 23-6 loss to the Bills — only the sick and twisted could’ve watched such a display until the end — the NFC North is 20-4 against opponents from outside the division. At 7-0, the Bears lead the way.</p><p>The only other divisions checking in with winning records against the rest of the league are the AFC North at 16-8 and the NFC West at 14-9.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-buccaneers-qb-baker-mayfield-accuse-mimicking-snap-count-cadence" target="_blank" >Bucs QB Baker Mayfield accuses Bears of mimicking his cadence</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/09/bears-qb-caleb-williams-must-use-4-interception-game-vs-buccaneers-to-to-keep-growing" >Bears QB Caleb Williams must use four-interception game vs. Buccaneers to keep growing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/08/bears-grades-buccaneers-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-chicago-sunday-night-soldier-field-nfl" >Bears’ grades are in. How did they do against the Buccaneers?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Brewers' Pat Murphy first to win three consecutive Manager of Year awards
entries.summary: <p>Pat Murphy from first-time World Series champion Milwaukee is the NL Manager of the Year, making him the first skipper from either league to win the award three years in a row.</p><p>Milwaukee has won the NL Central in all three seasons with Murphy as its manager after he spent eight seasons on Craig Counsell's staff. The Brewers led the majors this year with a franchise-record 103 wins during the regular season, then in the playoffs swept the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series and beat Tampa Bay in a five-game World Series.</p><p>Murphy, who turns 68 on Nov. 28, was in a hospital bed recovering from hip replacement surgery when he did interviews on MLB Network before and after the announcement.</p><p>Balloting by the Baseball Writers' Association of America was conducted before the postseason and announced Tuesday night.</p><p>The other NL finalists were Philadelphia's Don Mattingly and Atlanta's Walt Weiss.</p><p>The Brewers play in Major League Baseball's smallest market and have a payroll in the bottom half of the majors, but have had the best record in the big leagues each of the past two seasons.</p><p>After sweeping the NLCS for their first World Series berth since their only other one in 1982, Murphy celebrated by saying the Dodgers had Hall of Famers but his team had gamers.</p><p>Only three other managers have won the award three times in the same organization. Bobby Cox, one of three four-time winners along with Buck Showalter and Tony La Russa, earned three with the Atlanta Braves (1991, 2004 and 2005). Cox is also the only other back-to-back NL winner.</p><p>Terry Francona was a three-time winner with Cleveland (2013, 2016 and 2022), while Dusty Baker won three times with the San Francisco Giants (1993, 1997 and 2000).</p><p>Murphy got 20 of 30 first-place votes and finished with 124 points. Weiss came in second with seven first-place votes and 86 points.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/10/white-sox-will-venable-named-al-manager-of-the-year" >White Sox’ Will Venable named AL Manager of the Year</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Peoples Gas customers to get bill credits in settlement over surcharges from pipe-replacement program
entries.summary: <p>As Chicago residents begin turning their heat back on for the winter months, those who warm their homes with natural gas from Peoples Gas will see relief on their November bills.</p><p>Customers of the Chicago gas utility will see $56.18 in credits, thanks to a settlement the utility reached with the office of Attorney General Kwame Raoul this spring. The credits will be reflected through reductions on two line items on customer bills through Dec. 3, split roughly equally between the two sources.</p><p>Customers will also receive approximately $42 in credits in both 2027 and 2028 from the $125 million settlement.</p><p>“Every dollar customers save can make a meaningful difference, especially as the winter heating season begins,” Maria Bocanegra, president of Peoples Gas and North Shore Gas, said in a statement. “We remain committed to providing safe, reliable service and pursuing opportunities that deliver value for the customers we serve.”</p><p>The settlement stems from concerns raised by Raoul’s office and consumer advocates regarding the costs of Peoples Gas’ ongoing pipe retirement program, which is intended to replace over 1,000 miles of old iron pipes that carry natural gas underneath Chicago.</p><p>The attorney general’s office alleged Peoples Gas, in doing the work, imprudently incurred costs, which are passed onto customers. According to a statement from the office announcing the settlement, Peoples Gas customers paid an excessive surcharge for qualified infrastructure investments from 2017 through 2023.</p><p>As a result of the settlement, Peoples Gas also agreed to remove $130 million in capital investments. Since those costs are paid by consumers over time, it is expected to save customers over $350 million.</p><p>It also requires Peoples Gas to implement further accountability and transparency measures in its pipe retirement program, including competitive bidding for contracts over $25,000 and documenting and approving all cost changes greater than $5,000.</p><p>“These bill credits are good news for Peoples Gas customers who have suffered so much financial pain because of the utility’s wasteful spending,” Citizens Utility Board Executive Director Sarah Moskowitz said in a statement following the settlement announcement.</p><p>Financial assistance programs are available for Peoples Gas customers struggling with energy bills, including local and federal grants and bill reductions up to 83%, according to the utility company. More information can be found at <a class="Link" href="https://www.peoplesgasdelivery.com/payment-bill/assistance" target="_blank" >https://www.peoplesgasdelivery.com/payment-bill/assistance</a> or by calling 866-556-6001.</p><p></p>

entries.title: White Sox remain set on adding impact starting pitching, even after shifting Grant Taylor to rotation
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> are taking their best reliever in 24-year-old fireballer Grant Taylor, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/10/white-sox-moving-relief-ace-grant-taylor-to-the-rotation-hagen-smith-will-remain-in-the-bullpen" target="_blank" ><u>and moving him to the rotation</u></a>. If general manager Chris Getz has his way, it will only mark the beginning of the club’s efforts to upgrade their starting pitching.</p><p>“It's our top priority,” said Getz during Tuesday’s media availability at the MLB general manager meetings. “We feel pretty good about the depth, but we do want to find ways to upgrade the quality of the innings in the rotation.”</p><p>For Taylor, it’s the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/04/grant-taylor-is-carrying-the-white-sox-this-postseason-will-he-do-it-as-a-starter-in-the-future-kyle-teel-chris-getz-will-venable-brian-bannister-zach-bove" target="_blank" ><u>next step in a development plan</u></a> that aimed to gradually push his workload toward starting during the 2026 season, and a reward for proving he can stay healthy after arm injuries marred his collegiate career and initial introduction to professional baseball. For the White Sox, it’s just part of addressing the glaring need that dominated their playoff strategy.</p><p>As Getz noted, it’s easy to list names that have, could or even should start for the Sox next year — Davis Martin, Noah Schultz, David Sandlin, Luis Castillo, Anthony Kay — and quickly reach a total larger than five. But the Sox finished their postseason run without a pitcher they trusted to use as a traditional starter — or as close as they come to it — beyond Sean Burke. In adding Taylor’s elite closer-level stuff to the rotation, and their pursuit of starters on the open market, that’s the category to which they’re truly looking to add.</p><p>“We've seen what Davis Martin has done, we feel like Noah Schultz is going to take another step,” Getz said, noting that Martin struggled with a right calf issue after a stellar start to 2026. “But yeah, we're certainly targeting individuals that we feel like can pitch in the middle, to the top of the rotation.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/5z6YB9-i5oQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="White Sox GM Chris Getz on free agency"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The starter depth is the path to explaining how unconcerned Getz sounded about replacing an All-Star caliber closer, beyond Hagen Smith staying in a multi-inning relief role that sounds akin to what Taylor did this past season. Every team adds relievers every winter, but Getz rated it as a lower priority; not even as pressing as a right-handed outfielder to replace Randal Grichuk, or a new backup behind catcher Kyle Teel.</p><p>More likely, the biggest bullpen reinforcements will come from arms who don’t make the cut for the White Sox starting five, and Getz didn’t start handicapping the race for spots in November.</p><p>Instead, despite the anticipation of a frenzied offseason with teams looking to fill needs before an anticipated lockout on Dec. 1, the Sox GM said no indicators of quickened pace have emerged. The club is taking meetings with agents, including Scott Boras, and expect to hire a replacement for departed assistant hitting coach Joel McKeithan soon. But Getz also said the 2027 payroll is still being determined, even if he spoke with the expectation he’ll have the budget room to get stuff done.</p><p>“I feel confident we're going to be able to sign some free agents,” Getz said. “[The money] will be there when it comes to a player we feel like will be a really great addition.”</p><p>It also might not need to come via free agency.</p><p>With William Bergolla Jr. and Caleb Bonemer expected in big league camp next spring — though the latter is working in the outfield and guaranteed to start in Triple-A — along with Roch Cholowsky and Billy Carlson in the lower minors, there’s a glut of infield talent throughout the organization. While Getz acknowledged he could one day draw from this surplus in a trade, he added that it’s “not something that I would say we're entertaining right now.”</p><p>The White Sox are trying to upgrade a playoff team, and under tighter timelines with a nearing lockout. At the same time, they’re preaching patience.</p><p>“That method has worked well for us,” Getz said. “We want to win more games, but how you go about that process is just as important.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/10/white-sox-will-venable-named-al-manager-of-the-year" >White Sox’ Will Venable named AL Manager of the Year</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Lawmakers consider independent oversight of state prisons
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Department of Corrections might have to start answering to an independent watchdog. </p><p>The state corrections department has long been dogged by accusations of substandard medical care, intolerable living conditions and a lack of transparency. In its defense, department officials have pointed to several internal accountability measures that monitor the state's detention facilities and try to improve conditions. </p><p>But some state lawmakers say that's not enough. </p><p>A bill before the Illinois General Assembly would create an "independent corrections ombudsperson" responsible for monitoring and inspecting state detention facilities; investigating unresolved complaints from people incarcerated, their loved ones and prison staff; collecting and analyzing data on deaths, assaults, lockdowns and staff vacancies; and releasing reports to the public detailing their findings. </p><p>"The need for this oversight is clear," state Rep. Kevin John Olickal, D-Chicago, the bill's sponsor, said during a Tuesday committee hearing about the legislation. "Under our current system, we are relying on IDOC to investigate complaints about IDOC. We are asking the department to hold itself accountable, and that is not a sufficient hurdle." </p><p>Among the issues advocates and lawmakers say needs more oversight is how health care is delivered in state facilities. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/02/28/health-care-illinois-prisons-consent-decree" target="_blank" >A Chicago Sun-Times investigation</a> into healthcare conditions within state prisons found the state’s critically understaffed facilities struggle to deliver proper correctional medicine to the tens of thousands of incarcerated people in their care.</p><p>Nineteen states and Washington, D.C., each have an ombudsperson overseeing their corrections departments. Illinois established one to oversee the state Department of Juvenile Justice in 2014. </p><p>"It's time we bring the same level of accountability to our adult correctional facilities," Olickal said. "I recognize that IDOC faces significant challenges, particularly when it comes to staffing and resources, but these operational deficiencies cannot excuse failures to uphold constitutional protections or ensure basic safety."</p><p>Also at Tuesday's hearing before the Illinois House Restorative Justice & Public Safety Committee were prison reform advocates, out-of-state experts on prison oversight and IDOC's director, along with three department leaders. </p><p>Jennifer Vollen-Katz is director of the John Howard Association, the state's only independent prison oversight organization. At the hearing, she shared how her organization is allowed into the state's detention facilities to gather information and shed light on what’s happening in state prisons. </p><p>"However, there's a lot that we cannot do," Vollen-Katz said. "We are unable to investigate. We are unable to show up unannounced. Have access 24/7. We lack the mandate that allows for robust oversight that can make an even bigger difference in our prison system, both for the people who are incarcerated and the people who work inside our facilities." </p><p>An independent oversight system would give incarcerated people a meaningful way to have their concerns addressed beyond the current internal grievance process, said Byron Merriwether with Restore Justice. </p><p>"A grievance is the only way for an individual and IDOC to address their problems when they're being mistreated by staff," Merriweather said. "But this process is ineffective due to the grievance being thrown away, ignored or not being investigated." </p><p>Later during the hearing, IDOC Director Latoya Hughes said her department has plenty of oversight. She brought along the department's chief inspector, chief of compliance and chief of investigations to make her point. </p><p>"Oversight is important," Hughes said. "An additional oversight entity is not necessary when IDOC is subject to already extensive, multilayered oversight from independent external entities, the courts, federal regulatory requirements and our own internal compliance functions."</p><p>She said a state ombudsperson office would draw resources away from those existing oversight functions. Instead, she called for more support to go directly to IDOC. </p>

entries.title: Illinois hemp ban delayed — but only for some businesses
entries.summary: <p>Chicago consumers of hemp-derived THC products will have at least another week to stock up on beverages, edibles and other offerings at select breweries and retailers.</p><p>A statewide ban on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/11/07/chicago-businesses-bracing-state-hemp-thc-ban" >intoxicating hemp products</a> was set to take effect on Thursday, but an emergency motion filed last week by an industry trade group extends the deadline to at least Nov. 19, when their lawsuit will be heard by U.S. District Judge Martha Pacold.</p><p>Until then, the six plaintiffs and members of the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association will remain open and operational, according to ILHAA President Craig Katz. The trade group represents about 250 hemp businesses in the state.</p><p>“All the plaintiffs, including all the members of our association, are still allowed to sell federally compliant THC products,” said Katz, who also serves as government relations and compliance manager at MNG 2005, a plaintiff that operates 14 Illinois stores under the CBD Kratom brand.</p><p>A complete list of the eligible businesses wasn't available but includes companies such as CBD Botanicals in Springfield, Cubbington’s Cabinet in Roscoe Village and Green Street Distro, a hemp product distributor in Bridgeview.</p><p>In June, Gov. JB Pritzker signed a wide-ranging bill overhauling <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/06/15/illinois-hemp-delta-8-cannabis-regulation-bill" >cannabis and hemp regulations</a>, including reclassfiying hemp products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC as cannabis. The state’s timetable mimicked federal guidelines set in President Donald Trump’s 2025 spending bill that also outlawed hemp potency limits beyond 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. </p><p>While the federal deadline was recently extended to Dec. 11, Illinois is still following the original November deadline. So companies not covered by the lawsuit must stop selling and manufacturing hemp-derived THC products by Thursday or risk fines and other enforcement actions. This also means consumers will need to visit a licensed cannabis dispensary to purchase hemp THC products over the federal potency threshold.</p><p>South Loop Market owner Anas Masoud was alerted on Monday that his Logan Square store is allowed to continue selling hemp THC-infused beverages until at least 5 p.m. on Nov. 19.</p><p>“Hopefully, they extend it for a longer period of time,” he said. “Any little bit will be great. We’re all struggling.”</p><p>Until then, he’s added more inventory of hemp-derived THC beverages at his store, and he's offering shoppers a 25% discount. He said one frequent customer purchased two cases on Tuesday.</p><p>“Consumers are stocking up, and of course, they're getting a great deal because it's discounted,” he said.</p><div Fritz said.</p><p>The ban is expected to cut business at several restaurants, bars, retailers, manufacturers and entertainment venues across the city, particularly at a challenging time when alcohol consumption is at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2025/12/03/chicago-is-a-drinkers-paradise-even-for-the-sober-and-the-sober-curious-among-us" >record lows</a>.</p><p>“We Dosed, which makes THC emulsion ingredients for about 50 Illinois beverage brands, breweries and restaurants.</p><p>He also co-founded Rogers Park-based hemp-infused beverage brand Plift, which joined Perfectly Dosed in the lawsuit.</p><p>“The consequences of this ban are his responsibility and we hope he listens to the millions of Illinois adults who want to see THC beverages regulated like alcohol,” McElFresh said.</p><p>The 2018 Farm Bill removed hemp from the list of federally controlled substances and legalized its production as an agricultural commodity. But it also created a loophole allowing manufacturers to produce intoxicating hemp-derived products, with some infused with synthetics and unknown compounds, prompting consumer safety concerns nationwide.</p><p>Opponents often cite the lack of product testing, age verification for purchases, unregulated online marketplaces and integrating potentially dangerous synthetics in products.</p><p>“It's important to note that as an industry, we have been asking for regulation for years now,” Katz said. “We understand the consumer safety aspects.”</p><p>After Thursday, Illinois will be one of more than 20 states with some restrictions or an all out ban on the sale or production of hemp-derived THC products. </p><p>Missouri has already ramped up enforcement before its hemp product ban goes into effect Thursday, filing at least four lawsuits against retailers accused of selling marijuana products billed as hemp.</p><p>Ohio in March enacted a similar ban, which has propped up sales at licensed dispensaries, according to state sales data. </p><p>In Texas, legal battles waged for years over the legality and sale of intoxicating hemp products, culminating in a statewide ban in July. Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick led the crusade and campaigned on prohibition.</p><p>“I’m not going to legalize marijuana in Texas. And if people want to vote me out of office for that, so be it,” he said at a news conference last year. </p><p>Patrick lost his seat in the midterm elections to Democrat Vikki Goodwin, who said Tuesday she favors THC regulation over a ban.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/11/07/chicago-businesses-bracing-state-hemp-thc-ban" >How Chicago businesses are bracing for the state’s hemp ban</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Burnham Prize winners seek to make State Street great again
entries.summary: <p>It's been 30 years since the old State Street pedestrian mall was put out of its misery — a bold move that revived the "great street" and gave the Loop a bit more spark.</p><p>The 1996 makeover did things like reintroduce car traffic and upgrade landscaping and street furniture. State Street's whole vibe was changed. And the thoroughfare started to come alive.</p><p>But that was a generation ago. Today's State Street, slapped around by changing retail patterns and a pandemic that drained it and the Loop of many of its workers and shoppers, is again in need of bold moves and visionary planning.</p><p>Could help be on the way? </p><p>Under the theme "The Future of State," the Chicago Architectural Club awarded its 2026 Burnham Prize to an ambitious and thought-provoking proposal to revitalize State Street.</p><p>Called "Thickness: From Corridor to Urban Field" by the Argentinian architecture firm Andres Moroni Arquitecto, the proposal includes turning the never-used $400 million transit superstation space beneath Block 37 into a cultural and performance center.</p><p>The proposals "Unlocking State Street" by Chicago's Norbert Schlotter and "Civic Mischief" by the Virginia-based architecture firm Gluten took second and third place, respectively.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </div><p>The three schemes were awarded at a Tuesday evening event at the Chicago Architecture Foundation.</p><p>In addition to using the failed Block 37 station — built in 2009 to provide high-speed express train service to O'Hare and Midway airports — "Thickness" calls for greening rooftops on State Street and turning plazas and underground spaces into civic and gathering places.</p><p>A surface parking lot on Wabash Avenue, between Balbo Drive and Harrison Street, would become a landscaped green space with trees, walking paths and rolling topography.</p><p>"It has to be not just a corridor but something larger and very [Daniel] Burnham-like," former Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events Commissioner Mark Kelly, who served as the competition’s adviser, said of State Street.</p><p>"That Wabash and Dearborn have to be incorporated [and] the streets intersecting State Street," Kelly, a longtime advocate of the thoroughfare, said. "It's not just one element or one place, but it's taking on the totality of the setting that is around State Street."</p><p>An intriguing aspect of the "Unlocking State Street" proposal suggests a brighter future for the Century and Consumers buildings at 202 and 220 S. State St., respectively.</p><p>The vintage skyscrapers have sat vacant and rotting since being bought by the U.S. General Services Administration in 2005, partly because the federal government sees the redeveloped buildings as a security risk to the Dirksen Federal Courthouse just to the west.</p><p>"Unlocking State Street" challenges the security issue by creating a more open federal plaza, reusing the two buildings and constructing a bright red, super-tall mixed-use tower between them.</p><p>"It thumbs its nose at what the GSA came up with, which is to tear the down buildings to make [a security buffer]," Chicago Architecture Center CEO Eleanor Gorski, a Burnham Prize jury member, said. "This architect is saying, 'No, think about it this way instead,' and introduce people into the site. Having more people actually activates it, and you need less in terms of public safety. That provokes a conversation about the nature of those federal buildings and the plaza."</p><p>The architecture firm Gluten's "Civic Mischief" proposes art, pop-up shops, community spaces and other amenities to add more fun and whimsy along and around State Street — an important factor to include.</p><p>The Chicago Architecture Club and World Business Chicago will next put the proposals on display at the Chicago Architecture Center, 111 E. Wacker Drive.</p><p>The first-place winner receives $3,000. Second place gets $2,000, while third place takes home $1,000. And $100 goes to each of the 2026 Burnham Prize submittals that will be exhibited at the Chicago Architecture Center.</p><p>What happens to the proposals beyond that is anyone's guess.</p><p>But we know this: If State Street is going to measurably improve, it's time for Mayor Brandon Johnson to stand up and make its revival a signature project of his administration.</p><p>And say it with his chest, too. Just as former Mayor Lori Lightfoot did with Invest South/West, Mayor Rahm Emanuel with the Chicago Riverwalk and Mayor Richard M. Daley with Millennium Park.</p><p>The entire city benefits culturally, economically and socially from a vibrant and healthy State Street.</p><p>Getting there means going through the 2026 Burnham Prize winners, and perhaps, picking the best ideas and concepts, then rallying the city, business, philanthropic, arts and cultural sectors — and his own departments — around a new and executable State Street revitalization plan.</p><p>And while we're at it, add the Chicago Loop Alliance's wide-ranging <a class="Link" href="https://loopchicago.com/business-in-the-loop/elevate-state/#elevatestate" target="_blank" >Elevate State plan</a> from 2023 to the mix.</p><p>Chicago is known for making no little plans, so congrats to the winners and to the Chicago Architecture Club for making this year's Burnham Prize happen.</p><p>The city is best known for what it builds, and the remaking of State Street ought to be Chicago's next big thing — if the "fifth floor" provides the vision and leadership to make it happen.</p>

entries.title: Feds question 'Broadview 6' judge's authority as clash over top prosecutor's testimony inches closer
entries.summary: <p>The Justice Department on Tuesday<b> </b>questioned the authority of a federal judge<b> </b>to hold a “mini-trial”<b> </b>over the wreckage of Chicago’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six”</a> case, further signaling a likely challenge before the judge can put U.S. Attorney Andrew<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>on the witness stand.</p><p>Associate<b> </b>Attorney<b> </b>General<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" target="_blank" >Stanley<b> </b>Woodward</a><b> </b>also raised the possibility that Boutros and other federal prosecutors might invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. It’s the second time in six weeks<b> </b>that a Justice Department official left that possibility on the table.</p><p>“The court has presented the United States Attorney and his subordinates with a Catch-22,” Woodward wrote<b> </b>in a five-page<b> </b>court filing<b> </b>Tuesday. “They can testify and risk prosecution, or they can assert their rights under the Fifth Amendment and risk antagonizing the court.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/06/broadview-6-hearing-set-to-rock-chicago-federal-courthouse-but-doj-official-could-intervene" >Broadview 6 hearing set to rock Chicago federal courthouse, but DOJ official could intervene</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Boutros is considered the Chicago area’s top federal law enforcement official, but he and others now face the possibility of sanctions or a criminal contempt finding<b> </b>in U.S. District Judge<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" >April<b> </b>Perry’s</a> courtroom.</p><p>Perry has yet to make any such finding. But she's<b> </b>previously<b> </b>cited her "inherent authority to sanction abuse of the judicial process."</p><p>Woodward is the Justice Department’s third-highest ranking official. He’s yet to formally challenge Perry’s<b> </b>Nov. 2 order<b> </b>that<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>testify, but he seemed to take a step in that direction Tuesday by<b> </b>asking<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>to<b> </b>clarify<b> </b>her<b> </b>authority<b> </b>for doing so.</p><p>The judge does not appear to be backing down, either. Rather, she<b> </b>complained<b> </b>on the court docket Tuesday<b> </b>that<b> </b>records<b> </b>turned<b> </b>over<b> </b>to her Monday<b> </b>by the Justice Department fell short of what she’d asked for<b> </b>a month ago.</p><p>Among other things, Perry wanted to see an Oct. 14, 2025, email<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>received, in order to test his claim that he<b> </b>didn’t know about alleged misconduct<b> </b>by his team in the “Broadview Six” case. She asked not only for the email, but metadata, “including read receipts, delivery status, and message tracking logs.”</p><p>The Justice Department claimed<b> </b>to have turned responsive<b> </b>records<b> </b>over<b> </b>to Perry on Monday. But Tuesday, she<b> </b>complained<b> </b>that she’d received “two 1-page emails”<b> </b>in PDF format — with no metadata.</p><p>“The point of requesting the 10/14/2025 email and attachment was to provide corroboration for U.S. Attorney Boutros’ claim that he had not read them,” Perry wrote. “The government’s chosen manner of production thus sheds no light on the only relevant issue.”</p><div further into unprecedented territory. Perry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/02/fbi-boutros-depodesta-broadview-six" target="_blank" >clearly doesn’t believe</a> what Boutros has told her about the disastrous “Broadview Six” case — but Woodward suggested there’s little she can do about it.</p><p>“No authority exists for a federal judge to hold a mini-trial dedicated to uncovering and assessing evidence with criminal sanctions on the table,” Woodward wrote.</p><p>Perry<b> </b>has said Boutros<b> </b>must<b> </b>testify<b> </b>Nov. 16, unless<b> </b>attorneys<b> </b>agree<b> </b>on another date for the hearing to happen<b> </b>by<b> </b>Nov. 24. She also ordered three rank-and-file prosecutors who worked the “Broadview Six” case to testify.</p><p>The case revolved around a protest outside an immigration holding facility in west suburban Broadview in September 2025. It occurred at the height of the Trump administration’s Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >case collapsed</a> in May after Perry discovered<b> </b>alleged misconduct by Boutros’ staff while seeking an indictment from a grand jury. The initial controversy revolved around<b> </b>the conduct of a veteran rank-and-file prosecutor.</p><p>But Perry has turned her attention to the accuracy of two claims<b> </b>made by the feds<b> </b>last spring.</p><p>The judge asked<b> </b>Boutros’ office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/09/feds-appear-to-hide-name-of-government-lawyer-in-new-broadview-six-court-filing" target="_blank" >to turn over records</a><b> </b>by Oct. 30<b> </b>that would help her test them. Instead, Woodward<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/30/controversial-doj-boss-takes-reins-in-tainted-broadview-6-case-stymies-judges-inquiry" target="_blank" >inserted himself</a> into the case<b> </b>that day, in what appeared to be an effort to stymie Perry’s inquiry.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" >‘Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>On Monday, he<b> </b>filed<b> </b>notice<b> </b>that<b> </b>he’d<b> </b>turned over records<b> </b>that were<b> </b>“responsive”<b> </b>to one such request — dealing with Boutros’ email.</p><p>The day the “Broadview Six” case fell apart, Boutros<b> </b>told<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>he<b> </b>only<b> </b>learned of certain misconduct<b> </b>by his team<b> </b>in late April. But later, he<b> </b>acknowledged<b> </b>he’d<b> </b>received<b> </b>a<b> </b>transcript<b> </b>by email on Oct. 14, 2025, documenting the misconduct at issue.</p><p>Boutros said he didn’t remember reading it. That’s why Perry wanted to see the metadata and read receipts —<b> </b>to test Boutros’ claim.</p><p>The second point at issue revolved around whether the White House played any role in the case.</p><p>Boutros’ team told Perry in March there were “no communications of any nature from, to, or with anyone outside [the U.S. attorney’s office] (other than the local FBI investigators assigned to the case) regarding any investigatory or charging decisions.</p><p>“To be crystal clear, this specifically includes anyone in the White House” or at Justice Department headquarters in Washington, prosecutors wrote.</p><p>Perry originally <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/07/broadview-ice-kat-abughazaleh-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >took the feds at their word</a><b> </b>that the communications don’t exist. But Boutros’ team has since suggested otherwise. So, mirroring the feds’ language, Perry<b> </b>on<b> </b>Oct. 9 asked<b> </b>them<b> </b>to turn over records<b> </b>of any such communication.</p><p>Rather than deny they exist, the Justice Department<b> </b>on Monday cited privilege<b> </b>to withhold such records.</p>

entries.title: Ben Brown undergoes neck surgery, further muddying Cubs’ already unclear starting-pitching picture for 2027
entries.summary: <p>LAS VEGAS — A new wrinkle has been thrown into the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ starting-pitching plans for next season.</p><p>Right-hander Ben Brown underwent neck surgery Monday, general manager Carter Hawkins said Tuesday at the GM meetings, the latest turn in what’s become a long-running story surrounding the 27-year-old’s nagging injury.</p><p>Brown was initially misdiagnosed with an osteoma, or bone growth, in 2024, his season ending early due to the injury. After a 2025 campaign that saw poor results (an ERA near 6.00), he was excellent, posting a 1.70 ERA in eight starts last season before things came to an abrupt end in June with what was finally determined to be a stress fracture in a vertebra in his neck. Though he attempted to return by season’s end, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-ben-brown-injury-setback-neck-fracture-playoff-bullpen-2027-starting-rotation" >he experienced a setback in August</a>, officially ending his campaign.</p><p>As he recovers from the surgery, the Cubs expect him to start throwing early next year and to be ready to pitch in major league games somewhere near the middle of the 2027 season.</p><p>“It’s an aggressive move, but Ben’s an aggressive player that has a lot of hopes for his career. And we have a lot of hopes for him, too,” Hawkins said. “We’re just very optimistic that this is going to be able to help him log the type of innings that he’ll need to log to be the elite pitcher that he can be.</p><p>“He’s got some work to do, but we feel really good about the prognosis.”</p><p>The news on Brown further muddies what was already an unclear picture of what the Cubs’ rotation will look like next year.</p><p>All five of the pitchers who finished the 2026 season in the starting rotation are free agents, and the in-house candidates to fill some of the vacancies are coming off significant injuries, a group that already included Brown. Left-hander Justin Steele finished last season healthy but hasn’t pitched in two years, while righty Cade Horton is on the comeback trail from Tommy John surgery.</p><p>The news on Brown doesn’t exactly intensify what was already Priority No. 1 for Jed Hoyer’s front office. The team president made it clear during his end-of-season press conference that the Cubs will be dedicating the majority of their focus — and resources — to pitching this offseason, and starting pitching, in particular, seems a bigger need than the relief corps, though that unit could also get a significant makeover.</p><p>“It’s no secret how many guys are coming off our books, just from a free-agent perspective, and then there’s uncertainty around the injuries,” Hawkins said. “We’re going to be looking to bring in several arms. … We’re going to make sure we’re getting good deals, but we’ll be active in that market.</p><p>“You have to make a good projection on how many innings those arms [returning from injuries] are going to give you. You certainly aren’t penciling all those guys in for 220 innings. That plays into the calculation of how many arms we need and what we’re looking to do.”</p><p>After <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/27/cubs-ben-brown-neck-injury-recovery-timeline-starting-rotation-pitching-injuries-justin-steele-rotation" >finally getting clarity</a> surrounding what had been bothering him for years, Brown talked last summer about the potential for significant changes to how he pitches that could prevent the injury from popping up again.</p><p>After surgery, the Cubs are hopeful this can be put in the rear-view mirror.</p><p>“We’re hopeful we get a 100-percent Ben Brown next year after he gets healthy, and hopefully we put some of these neck issues behind us,” Hawkins said. “The doctors gave him a really good prognosis that he’s going to be able to pitch for us next year and for a long time after that. Hopefully, that stabilizes things and puts him in a really good place.</p><p>“This isn’t something that is usual or a normal type of surgery, but at the same time, we are very confident that he’s going to pitch for us next year.”</p>

entries.title: Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/arts-and-entertainment-general-news-61ce97fcb3cc476f86c4ab60aed712ec" target="_blank" >Stacy Keach,</a> one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.</p><p>Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.</p><p>“I was feeling no pain,” the actor <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2017/06/08/stacy-keach-talks-about-his-onstage-heart-attack-at-goodman-theatre/" target="_blank" >told the Chicago Tribune</a> then of his seemingly traumatic experience. “The whole time, I was hoping that I was just in the middle of an actor’s nightmare, and that I would soon wake up and find myself back in the position where I knew what I was doing again.”</p><p>Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.</p><p>Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating “World's Most Amazing Videos” on TV. He played a deranged colonel in “The Ninth Configuration” (also known as “Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane”), led the TV show “Titus," had a role in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama “Nebraska,” and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama “Blue Bloods.” Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/jay-kelly-movie-review-clooney-82cff4184b00ceef38dea7d55dac35ae" target="_blank" >in “Jay Kelly.”</a></p><p>Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie “Lone Rider,” said in a post on X that Keach was a “consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him.”</p><h4>From TV to stage</h4><p>He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries “Mistral's Daughter,” a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel “Princess Daisy,” Barabbas in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/a05dc1bad5774b049fdaf254ef909206" target="_blank" >Franco Zeffirelli’s</a> “Jesus of Nazareth” and Maj. Jonas Steele in “The Blue and the Gray.” He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds (16 kilograms).</p><p>Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play “Indians,” played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in “King Lear” on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in “The Kentucky Cycle” in 1993, “The Country Wife” in 1965 and “Other Desert Cities” in 2011.</p><p>He also headed the national touring company cast of “Frost/Nixon,” portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with “Sleuth” with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of “King Lear” at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for “Pamplona,” a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/general-news-56fb3d5fef374858a1bcd274d0ca20e8" target="_blank" >to the run’s cancellation.</a></p><h4>A pivotal arrest</h4><p>While he was still doing “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer” (later titled “The New Mike Hammer”), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.</p><p>“As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, “All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage.” He added: “It was the lowest moment of my life.”</p><p>He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book “The Blue and the Gray.”</p><p>The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.</p><p>In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, “The Long Riders.” He said the experience was “very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.”</p><p>Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.</p><h4>Keach’s life after prison</h4><p>His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, “Intimate Strangers” <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/teri-garr-dies-be39482a60724c5bb81bbd8f34dfaf2d" target="_blank" >with Teri Garr,</a> and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, “The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer,” also played well, and then the “Mike Hammer” series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS' 1986-87 schedule.</p><p>Many years later, in the TV series “Prison Break” that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.</p><p>Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.</p><p>In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in “Hamlet” with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.</p><p>Keach made his film debut in 1968 in “The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter” and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in “Fat City” and “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean” and had roles in “American History X” with Edward Norton and “The Bourne Legacy.” He played a tough trucker in “Roadgames,” was electrocuted in “Children of the Corn” and a robot removed his heart in “Class of 1999.”</p><p>His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog.</p><p>“Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora,” said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. “He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.”</p>

entries.title: Man found fatally shot in Belmont Cragin alley
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot in the Belmont Cragin neighborhood Tuesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 19, was found with a single gunshot wound to his back in an alley near the 2500 block of North Monitor Avenue at 6:21 p.m., police said. </p><p>He was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>No one is in custody. An investigation is underway.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Twenty years married and still a virgin
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a 59-year-old married virgin male. My wife has an IUD for medical reasons. She thinks it's the man's job to initiate sex. She has never shown any interest in sex in nearly 20 years of marriage. I love her, but I am ready to divorce her.</p><p>I do not want to go through life without a sex life, let alone die a virgin. We have no money for therapy. She's going to be 51 soon. I have been told by different women that it's just not in her, and she'll never be interested. What should I do? — <i>WANTING MORE</i></p><p><b>DEAR WANTING MORE:</b> This may seem like a silly question, but have you tried to initiate sex? Your letter is a bit vague on that point. It's not the "job" of one partner or the other, but someone has to get the ball rolling. A more important question is this: Did your wife tell you she was not interested in sex before you got married? Did the two of you never discuss it?</p><p>Ask your wife directly if she thinks she'll ever be willing to take this step with you. If the answer is no, please understand that it's OK to end a relationship with someone — even if you love them — if they are not willing to give you what you need.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son-in-law takes my granddaughter for a walk every day. They live in a nice area, but he insists on carrying a loaded gun in the stroller. My daughter doesn't seem to question this, and if I press either one, I get the impression that they will cut off my access to my granddaughter. What recourse, if any, do I have to protect the child from a senseless gun-related accident? — <i>FEARFUL IN PHOENIX</i></p><p><b>DEAR FEARFUL:</b> It's sad that, despite living in a nice neighborhood, your son-in-law feels so vulnerable. All you can do is try to ensure that he has a license to carry his gun and hope he has taken (and passed) a course in gun safety.</p><p>Readers who do not live in Arizona should check their own state and local laws. What this dad is doing may be legal in Phoenix, but it could land you in a heap of trouble in many other jurisdictions!</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Twenty years ago, I moved into a modest home owned by my sister to help her with expenses. Shortly after, she got a job promotion and transfer. I stayed, took care of repairs and paid her rent. A couple of years later, she signed it over to me as a Christmas present. I did put thousands of dollars and many hours of labor into repairs. If I sell it now, do I owe her a share of the profits? — <i>HANDYMAN IN ILLINOIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR HANDYMAN:</b> You do not owe your sister a share of the profits for the house. She gave it to you, so it is yours to do with as you wish. If you would like to give her a portion of the proceeds to thank her for the opportunity, it's your choice.</p><p><b>DEAR VETERANS:</b> For your service to our nation, I salute you. My thanks to each of you on this Veterans Day. You personify patriotism, self-sacrifice and dedication to our country. I would also like to recognize your families for the sacrifices they, too, have made while you were serving your country. — <i>LOVE, ABBY</i></p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Keep veterans informed about educational opportunities
entries.summary: <p>All too few veterans come out of military service and pursue higher education. Only <a class="Link" href="https://vetsedsuccess.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/GI-Bill-First-Look-FINAL-AV1.pdf" target="_blank" >54%</a> of eligible enlisted veterans between 2009 and 2019 took advantage of the post-911 GI Bill to pay for higher education, according to the U.S. Census Bureau and other organizations.</p><p>So what about the other half? Without training and either a certificate or a diploma, they’re unlikely to be qualified for high-paying, upwardly mobile jobs. And veterans returning to civilian life generally take longer than others to find the right job, too. A U.S. Chamber of Commerce study found that <a class="Link" href="https://www.acp-usa.org/news/veterans-struggle-to-find-work-after-military-we-still-want-to-give-the-best-of-ourselves/" target="_blank" >53%</a> of veterans need at least four months to land a new role.</p><p>But if veterans pursue postsecondary education, they have a chance to move ahead faster and earn more. Therefore, they need to be made aware of federal financial assistance that’s available for traditional four-year universities and trade schools across the country that prepare electricians, nurses, welders, heating, ventilation and air conditioning technicians and truck drivers. </p><p>I should know. I was an intelligence analyst in the Army National Guard making a living as a pipe fitter. But I got laid off. So I decided to go back to school. I enrolled in Rockford Career College, a vocational institution, for an 18-month program to train as a surgical technologist. The post-9/11 GI Bill covered 60% of my tuition and provided a monthly stipend.</p><p>Result: I’ve gone from the Army to the operating room. I practice surgical technology at UnityPoint Health-Trinity, a nonprofit health system in Rock Island. I prep patients for surgery and assist surgeons performing procedures. My education isn't anywhere near over. I’m now studying to become a surgeon.</p><p>Make no mistake. College is hard. You have to go to class and study and do homework. But that’s where I rediscovered myself. I was president of the veterans club and student council and graduated as valedictorian.</p><p>I never could have done any of this without the support I got from family, friends, fellow students, faculty and career services staff. So I thank them. But let's all remember Wednesday that no one will ever deserve our heartfelt gratitude more than our veterans.</p><p><i>Logan McMullen, Army veteran and surgical technologist, East Moline</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Hang tight, America </h3><p>While I am grateful for the recent Democratic victories, I want to remind everyone to remain patient. The damage and challenges our country have experienced under the Trump administration will not be resolved overnight, nor will they be corrected in just two years.</p><p>Unfortunately, Donald Trump will remain president until 2028. The war in Iran may not end immediately, and our economy may not improve overnight. Additionally, many of the newly elected officials will not even take office until January.</p><p>In the meantime, I hope the House and Senate will begin developing and communicating a strong, focused legislative agenda. The American people deserve to know what the priorities are, what changes are being pursued and how success will be measured.</p><p>People want to see that their elected representatives are working, fighting for their communities and making a genuine effort to move our country forward.</p><p>Once again, America please be patient. The work ahead will take time, but the American people deserve to see progress.</p><p><i>Eli Washington, Chatham</i> </p><h3></h3><h3>Let’s turn a new page</h3><p>The electorate sent a clear message to the politicians in Washington, D.C., last week: We are tired of the daily drama with no results.</p><p>We finally had enough of their being blind and deaf to our needs and showed them that we ultimately have the power of the ballot box.</p><p>Now both parties have a chance to show that they heard and understand the message. I hope they don’t elect the same party leaders who've put us in this quagmire. But unfortunately on Tuesday, Jim Jordan was<a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/congress/republicans-reeling-election-choose-leadership-congress-rcna608300" target="_blank" > elected </a>as the House Republican leader. He, Chuck Schumer, Steve Scalise and others represent more of the same old petty turf wars and bickering.</p><p>Here's to hoping the new Congress brings us some new leaders to mark the end of the bipartisan mud slinging and start working for the people and not the party demigod.</p><p><i>Steven Fortuna, Naperville</i></p><h3>Clean swap </h3><p>Anything that's too expensive, too troublesome and/or just plain useless is often referred to as a white elephant. This concept merges perfectly with the Republican party's traditional symbol and what it has become since the midterm elections: "The White Elephant Party."</p><p><i>Chet Alexander, Alsip</i></p><h3>Tragic measles deaths </h3><p>With the year not yet over, there have been more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/07/cdc-has-recorded-more-than-5000-measles-cases-this-year/" target="_blank" >5,000 reported cases of measles</a>, a disease we thought had long been eliminated. There have been at least <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/Health/measles-cases-surpass-5000-us-infections-confirmed-45/story?id=137907591" target="_blank" >eight</a> people who have died from the disease this year, including unvaccinated children.</p><p>U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. may take some consolation in knowing that none of them had autism.</p><p><i>Dan McGuire, Bensenville</i></p><h3>Lukewarm headline </h3><p>Sexual assault is a horrific crime, and I am appalled at the University of Chicago's response to it. Monday's Sun-Times front page headline of WBEZ's Lisa Kurian Philip's story, "U. of C. rarely expels students responsible for sexual assault," underplays the seriousness of the problem. </p><p>Perhaps less whitewashing? Here are more accurate headlines: "U. of C. fails to protect students: rapists not expelled;" "U. of C. protects students guilty of sexual assault" or "U. of C. throws survivors under the bus, allows rapists to remain enrolled."</p><p><i>Joan Cordeniz, Lake Bluff</i></p><h3>Ladies first</h3><p>The next Illinois House speaker could be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/11/06/illinois-house-speaker-chris-welch-steps-down-female-replacement-contenders" target="_blank" >woman</a>? Yes please!</p><p><i>Gary Fox, Mount Prospect</i></p><h3>Not on thin ice?</h3><p>Hey Blackhawks fans, it’s time to get excited about the NHL playoffs and the Stanley Cup. The team figured a way to get back on track after the disastrous start to the regular season. You simply put the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/11/08/blackhawks-backup-goalie-change-arvid-soderblom-waivers" >backup goalie</a> on waivers and all your problems are solved.</p><p><i>Rick Kalin, Belmont Heights</i></p>

entries.title: Jury in California ensures accountability in deadly police shooting case
entries.summary: <p>Last week, Americans went to the polls to decide who should wield power in Washington D.C. Twelve days before Election Day, seven Americans serving on a federal jury offered their own answer.</p><p>They listened to a mother describe how San Bernardino County sheriff’s deputies killed her son. Then they held those deputies accountable.</p><p>Antonio “Tony” Garza Jr. was 44, a union mechanic and welder. He built his sister a nine-foot farm table. When his father became ill, Tony built him a wheelchair ramp and remodeled the bathroom so he could bathe. After his father died, Tony promised his mother, Matilde, he would take care of her. He lived a mile and a half away and visited almost daily.</p><p>You probably know somebody like Tony. The family member everyone calls when something breaks.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3b0000" name="module-3b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Tony also had bipolar disorder. As his illness worsened, his family struggled to get him treatment. He spent months in jail waiting for a mental-health bed that never materialized. After his release, Matilde took him to the county behavioral-health office. She testified that they turned him away because he wasn’t suicidal.</p><p>Less than two weeks later, deputies shot him dead.</p><p>On Feb. 5, 2023, deputies responding to a report of a fire at Tony’s property chased his pickup nearly 30 miles. Tony drove dangerously. When he finally stopped beside Interstate 10, he ran into the desert holding a golf club, shouting for deputies to shoot him.</p><p>Deputies Nicholas Kridner and Bill Abernathy testified that Tony raised the club threateningly and they feared for their lives. They fired 21 rounds in two volleys, striking him 12 times. Autopsy evidence documented wounds from behind and others inflicted while he was on the ground.</p><p>A passing motorist filmed part of the encounter. The deputies had no body cameras.</p><p>Matilde learned her son was dead from her daughters. No one from the sheriff’s department came to tell her.</p><p>The department found the shooting within policy. Neither deputy was disciplined or criminally charged. Abernathy became a detective; at trial, Kridner was introduced as soon to become one. Jurors also learned the department had rejected Kridner for dishonesty during hiring, then hired him anyway.</p><p>The Garza family was represented by a team of civil rights lawyers: Rebecca Brown, Brian Olney and David Clay Washington. Brown opened with a simple declaration: “Antonio Garza, Jr. did not need to die.” Olney delivered the closing argument. Washington, who had worked with young people in mental-health crises and challenged prison conditions in Alabama, confronted Kridner with a recording from his own belt.</p><p>Kridner had testified he couldn’t remember ordering Tony to “roll over” before the second volley. The jury heard the order. Kridner acknowledged giving it.</p><p>Eleven months after Tony’s death, the department’s deputies shot and killed Frank Glasgow, 57, after he called 911 saying he wanted police to kill him. Washington says Kridner was among the deputies who fired. The department said Glasgow charged a deputy with a knife.</p><p>Presiding over Tony’s case was Judge Consuelo Bland Marshall, a Black woman born in segregated Knoxville, Tennessee. She was one of four women in her class of 60 at Howard University School of Law. The Los Angeles city attorney’s office told her it didn’t hire women lawyers. She became its first. She later practiced with Johnnie Cochran. President Jimmy Carter appointed her to the federal bench in 1980; she eventually became that court’s first woman chief judge.</p><p>On Oct. 22, the seven jurors unanimously awarded Matilde and Tony’s estate $51.8 million, believed to be California’s largest police-shooting jury verdict. That included $10 million in punitive damages against the deputies. They also found a violation of Tony’s rights under the Americans with Disabilities Act.</p><p>“These jurors are the only accountability anyone has seen,” Washington told me.</p><p>The verdict may be appealed. No amount can bring Tony home. But from Southern California to Chicago, families deserve to know that a badge doesn’t put anyone beyond accountability.</p><p>When the news from the powers that be in Washington, D.C., makes us doubt our country’s promises, remember Matilde Garza. She once hiked through Joshua Tree with Tony while her granddaughter photographed the wildflowers. These days, she rarely leaves home. But she went to court, and seven strangers heard her son’s story and held the deputies accountable.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-be0000" name="module-be0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
