entries.title: Students at Illinois public universities deserve funding based on their unique needs
entries.summary: <p>There was a time when a high school diploma was the ticket to getting a good job that paid a decent wage and provided benefits. That time is over. Today the path to self-sufficiency is a college degree. Start by considering earnings potential. Back in 1979, the median earnings of a full-time worker with a bachelor’s degree were 38% greater on average than a high school grad’s. According to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, by 2024 that wage differential had ballooned to 84%.</p><p>That growth in wage differential is just one of many compelling indicia that demonstrate the increased value of gaining a postsecondary education. In fact, virtually all the data show that folks with college degrees have lower rates of unemployment, higher incomes and better life outcomes than do their peers who don’t complete college. A study by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research institute, even found that communities with more college-educated individuals enjoy lower crime rates, better overall health and higher wages for all workers — not just those with advanced degrees.</p><p>Yet despite all the documented benefits accruing to both individuals and communities from getting a college degree, state funding for higher education in Illinois has declined in real terms for decades. That disinvestment has been so substantial that even though state appropriations for higher education have increased in nominal dollars each of the last three fiscal years, after adjusting for inflation, total state funding for higher education at the end of fiscal year 2027 is projected to be 47.3%, or fully $2.362 billion less, than it was nearly 30 years ago in FY 2000, under Republican Gov. George Ryan.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-200000" name="module-200000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>The good news is, Illinois Senate Majority Leader Kimberly Lightford is providing some real visionary leadership on this issue. A couple of years ago, she co-chaired a legislatively established the Commission on Equitable Public University Funding. That commission was composed of legislators, independent policy experts and representation from each public university in the state. The commission, which — full disclosure — I also served on, issued a recommendation to the General Assembly on how to design an evidence-based formula that would “adequately, equitably, and stably fund public universities in this State.”</p><p>Lightford, together with colleagues in both chambers of the General Assembly, translated that recommendation into legislation, introduced as<a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=SB&DocNum=13&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=157103" target="_blank" > Senate Bill 13</a>. If enacted, SB 13 will represent the first ever research-based formula for funding public universities in Illinois history. According to Lightford, the formula supports core university operating functions, funds programs proven to attract and graduate traditionally underrepresented students, and will help reduce the cost of attending public universities for all students, while also eliminating barriers to both higher-ed access and completion based on income.</p><h3>Providing opportunity</h3><p>Lightford emphasized that “every Student in Illinois deserves the opportunity to go to college and get a degree, no matter their ZIP code, their family’s income, or which public university they attend. But Illinois’ historic approach to funding higher education doesn’t create that opportunity. The facts make it clear that to date, state funding for public universities in Illinois is uneven, and the students who need the most support often attend institutions with the fewest resources.” </p><p>Lightford noted that the evidence-based funding metrics in SB 13 reveal that as things stand today, Illinois’ public universities collectively have only 68.5% of the resources they need to serve students adequately. She lamented that “this gap isn’t fair, and it translates into higher tuition bills and larger debts for all students, while making it financially difficult for many low-income, first generation, and rural students to complete their degrees.”</p><p>During our conversation, Lightford stressed that SB 13 would directly redress the most troubling aspects of the state’s current, highly political and completely unscientific approach to funding public universities, by creating a student-centered formula that identifies the financial resources each university requires to both serve all its students well, irrespective of their backgrounds or specific learning needs, and satisfy its unique educational mission. </p><p>“Equity does not mean treating every institution the same,” Lightford insisted. “It means giving every student what they need to succeed academically. A first-generation student in Chicago, a rural student in southern Illinois and a working parent returning to school all deserve to attend a university that has the resources it takes to support them through graduation.”</p><p>Lightford explained that’s why SB 13 would focus new state investments on those public universities facing the greatest financial challenges, and crucially pair this heightened investment of taxpayer dollars with new transparency and accountability metrics to ensure every dollar supports student success.</p><p>Lightford ended our conversation with a simple request: that her colleagues pass SB 13 and give every Illinois student a fair shot at a self-sufficient future.</p><p><i>Ralph Martire is executive director of the Center for Tax and Budget Accountability, a nonpartisan fiscal policy think tank, and the Arthur Rubloff professor of public policy at Roosevelt University.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-670000" name="module-670000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Independent review of Cook County Jail can improve conditions, save lives
entries.summary: <p>As faith leaders representing multiple religious traditions, we are unified in the conviction that every human life possesses inherent worth and dignity. That includes those who are incarcerated and awaiting trial. </p><p>Over the last five years, Cook County has seen a dramatic increase in the number of people who have lost their lives while incarcerated in the Cook County Jail. A <a class="Link" href="https://projects.illinoisanswers.org/inside-illinois-jail-unusual-events/data/counties/cook/" target="_blank" >recent study</a> found that 85 people died in the jail between 2019 and 2025. In that time, the jail reported 13,192 extraordinary or unusual incidents and failed six of the nine Illinois Department of Corrections inspections.</p><p>In 2023 alone, 18 people, predominantly Black men, died in custody, marking the jail's highest mortality rate in at least three decades. <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/jail-deaths/2024/cook-county-jail-deaths-2023/" target="_blank" >An investigation by Injustice Watch</a> identified serious lapses in medical care and supervision preceding at least half of those deaths, raising urgent questions about institutional accountability and the adequacy of existing safeguards.</p><p>These are not simply statistics. Each number represents a human life, a grieving family and a community left to reckon with a loss that cannot be undone.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-200000" name="module-200000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>When the government takes custody of an individual, it assumes a profound responsibility for that person's safety and well-being. Incarceration may restrict a person's freedom, but it does not diminish their humanity, nor does it relieve public officials of their obligation to preserve life.</p><p>That responsibility is why, in September, we <a class="Link" href="https://drive.google.com/file/d/1tweZ3Xp-anVIZ-z_k-B1fOviYCJo2bg2/view?usp=sharing" target="_blank" >signed a letter</a> along with more than 70 faith leaders in calling on Cook County Board's Health and Hospitals Committee to pass and advance a <a class="Link" href="https://cook-county.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8136917&GUID=5E61B797-E087-43CC-A54C-869EC905E234&Options=Advanced&Search=" target="_blank" >resolution</a> that expresses support for an independent review of Cook County Jail. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/public-safety/2026/09/21/cook-county-jail-deaths-commissioners-board" >resolution</a>, which was introduced by Cook County Commissioner Tara Stamps and her co-sponsors, focuses on the health, safety, wellness and conditions of confinement.</p><p>Members of our coalition conveyed the urgency of this request before committee on Sept. 22. National jail experts also joined us, explaining the importance of independent scrutiny, a practice employed in other major jurisdictions and one with a history at Cook County Jail.</p><p>We had hoped the resolution would advance from committee to the full board. Instead, the committee went into executive session following discussion of legal concerns, and consideration of the resolution was deferred. Reports indicated that <a class="Link" href="https://illinoisanswers.org/2026/09/22/cook-county-board-defers-resolution-calling-for-independent-review-of-states-largest-jail/" target="_blank" >concerns about potential liability contributed to the difficulty in securing sufficient votes for its passage</a>.</p><p>We recognize that public officials have a responsibility to consider legal and financial consequences. But those concerns cannot be allowed to overshadow the fundamental obligation to protect human life. The public deserves a clear explanation of how delaying an independent review serves the interests of those in custody and the broader community.</p><p>Cook County has already spent <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/06/11/cook-county-settles-man-hanged-jail-cell/" target="_blank" >millions of dollars</a> settling lawsuits involving deaths and harm experienced by people in its custody. An independent review offers an opportunity to identify institutional failures, reduce preventable harm and potentially limit the financial and legal consequences of leaving those failures unaddressed. No financial consideration, however, should outweigh our responsibility to preserve human life.</p><h3>Protecting, preserving lives</h3><p>An independent examination of medical care, staffing, supervision, safety practices and institutional procedures could provide commissioners and the public with credible information needed to implement evidence-based improvements. Such a review should also lay the foundation for sustained transparency and meaningful accountability. Independent review is not inherently an attack on the sheriff's office or its personnel. Accountability is a necessary expression of responsible leadership and an essential means of preserving public trust.</p><p>Other cities, including Los Angeles, Philadelphia and New York, have established forms of independent jail oversight. As the operator of one of the nation's largest single-site jails, Cook County should recognize the importance of independent scrutiny in protecting human life.</p><p>While our theological traditions differ, we find common moral ground in the responsibility to preserve human life, uphold dignity and confront injustice. We are guided by the Jewish mandate to preserve the lives of those endangered; the Quranic teaching that saving one life is as though one has saved all humanity; the Buddhist call to extend compassion to all living beings; and Christian teachings that call believers to care for the incarcerated and speak on behalf of those whose voices are too often unheard.</p><p>These teachings remind us that justice is reflected not only in our individual conduct but also in the institutions we establish and the authority we entrust to public officials. Those of us entrusted with leadership, whether in the pulpit or public office, bear a responsibility to ensure that authority is exercised with integrity and accountability.</p><p>An independent review will not resolve every challenge facing Cook County Jail. But it is a necessary step toward understanding the circumstances surrounding preventable deaths and establishing reforms that can save lives.</p><p>We call on the County Board’s Health and Hospitals Committee to advance the resolution to the full board and demonstrate that protecting human life takes precedence over political and institutional interests.</p><p>Protecting human life is not a partisan obligation. It is a shared human responsibility.</p><p><i>The </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.jamarboydii.com/about" target="_blank" ><i>Rev. Jamar Boyd</i></a><i> is the pastor of Kenwood United Church of Christ.</i></p><p><i>Imam </i><a class="Link" href="https://tariqelamin.com/about" target="_blank" ><i>Tariq I. El-Amin</i></a><i> is the resident imam at Masjid Al-Taqwa.</i></p><p><i>Rabbi </i><a class="Link" href="https://ctschicago.academia.edu/RachelMikva" target="_blank" ><i>Rachel S. Mikva </i></a><i>is the Herman E. Schaalman professor in Jewish Studies and a senior faculty Fellow of the InterReligious Institute at Chicago Theological Seminary.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f10000" name="module-f10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: How a retired Chicago Army veteran found peace and purpose through baking
entries.summary: <p>At 4:30 a.m. Tuesday, with most of Chicago still asleep, Quinton McNair already was in the kitchen.</p><p>By 9 a.m., the 49-year-old had baked enough cookies, muffins and other treats to fill the display cases at his Hyde Park bakery. And McNair still had the rest of another long day ahead of him.</p><p>“We have a big day tomorrow for Veterans Day. I have a lot of veterans' catering orders,” McNair said. “After we get done with all of this, I'm going back to the kitchen and baking some more. So it's gonna be a long, long, long day.”</p><p>It is a far cry from his previous job. For 24 years, McNair was a helicopter mechanic in the Army, deploying to places across the world, including Kosovo, Bosnia, Afghanistan and Iraq. He also served as a drill sergeant and later as a sexual assault response coordinator for a brigade of about 3,500 soldiers.</p><p>But McNair, who describes himself as a “deeply serious, unserious person” these days, has found a different kind of mission in baking.</p><p>When he retired in 2019 and returned to Chicago, he worked to find his footing. After decades of military life, the structure and sense of responsibility that had defined his days were suddenly gone. He struggled with PTSD and depression, felt isolated during the COVID-19 pandemic and used alcohol to cope.</p><p>“I felt like I didn't have a purpose, or I didn't know what my purpose was,” he said.</p><p>Then, almost by accident, he found baking.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" McNair thought if he could fix helicopters, he could probably figure out a cookie. His first attempt was far from delicious. But he approached baking the way he had approached fixing aircraft: by studying the science behind each ingredient and experimenting with recipes.</p><p>His early attempts were so uneven he jokingly used the hashtag “Strugglebeard Bakery,” a reference to the beard he was trying to grow out after two decades of being clean-shaven in the Army.</p><p>Eventually, the cookies got better. Soon, community members and friends began asking him to bring baked goods to events and ship them across the country. In 2020, he started a business out of his home kitchen in Matteson. </p><p>Three years later, in October 2023, he opened the Hyde Park storefront.</p><p>On Tuesday afternoon, the bakery smelled of freshly baked sweets and coffee. Military-themed art adorned the walls, and the display cases held rows of cookies, brownies and muffins, with a plethora of coffee and tea options listed on the menu.</p><p>McNair has made a point of sourcing products from other small, Black and minority-owned businesses, from the coffee and honey to the candles and tea. For him, the bakery is about more than selling something sweet.</p><p>“The driving purpose and point behind the bakery is ... to be something purposeful for the community,” McNair said.</p><p> McNair shared his story on Brief But Spectacular, which is an Emmy-nominated interview series that airs on during PBS NewsHour. The profile is now available to watch on <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yIPHTTDA-to&utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >YouTube</a>. </p><p>Though he lives in Matteson, McNair chose Hyde Park to open the bakery because of its sense of community, where residents support local businesses and connect.</p><p>For the bakery's third anniversary in October, he organized a street festival by inviting community partners, performers and groups, including Brave Space Alliance and Kenwood Academy's band, to celebrate with him.</p><p>That commitment to community took shape before the bakery. After retiring from the Army, McNair briefly taught flight theory and helped develop curriculum at Aerostar Avion Institute, a Chicago organization that introduces young people to aviation. Watching its founder, Tammera Holmes, build an organization around giving young people opportunities helped him imagine a life of service outside the military.</p><p>“I was around these people who were using their business or their influence to do something good in the community,” McNair said. “They gave me the idea that when I finally opened up my place, I could do the same, too.”</p><div skills had not become obsolete. entries.title: Lawmakers hold hearing on investigation into deadly Illinois prison fires
entries.summary: <p>Representatives for prison workers and people incarcerated at Illinois’ Joliet Treatment Center described poor mental healthcare and unsafe conditions during a hearing held by state lawmakers Tuesday.</p><p>Legislators called the hearing in response to an investigation by <a class="Link" href="https://www.themarshallproject.org/2026/07/24/prison-fires-joliet-illinois-mental-health" target="_blank" ><u>The Marshall Project, WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times</u></a> that revealed 70 fires at the Joliet Treatment Center in recent years. The prison was designed to provide intensive mental health treatment, but men there said they were so despondent over conditions that they set their cells — or themselves — on fire. The consequences were often tragic: One man needed a skin graft, another lost a leg, and two died.</p><p>The joint hearing of the state House of Representatives’ <a class="Link" href="https://www.legistorm.com/organization/summary/143407/Illinois_House_Mental_Health_and_Addiction_Committee.html" target="_blank" >Mental Health and Addiction</a> and Restorative Justice and Public Safety committees was called by Democratic state Reps. Lindsey LaPointe and Kelly Cassidy, both of Chicago. Cassidy said she had long been frustrated with poor prison conditions in the state.</p><p>“‘We're trying’ is no longer going to be enough of an answer,” she said.</p><p>Illinois Department of Corrections Director Latoya Hughes testified that 47% people in the state’s prisons have mental illness, and correctional facilities were never designed to provide long-term treatment. Still, prison administrators said the access to psychiatrists at the Joliet prison was phenomenal, and men there can participate in group therapy and activities.</p><p>But an employee at the prison, as well as lawyers for incarcerated people, painted a very different picture before the dozens of people in attendance at the hearing in downtown Chicago.</p><p>Amanda Antholt, a lawyer who represents people incarcerated at the Joliet Treatment Center and managing attorney at the disability law firm Equip For Equality, said people there rarely get individual therapy. Instead, she said, they face harsh punishments. For example, she said officers pepper spray people for engaging in self-harm.</p><p>Sheena McClain, a Joliet employee and AFSCME local union president, said the facility had failed to take actions to fight fires, such as installing sprinklers. She said employees are asked “to rush into smoke-filled cells, in some cases with little more than an N-95 mask to protect them.”</p><p>The inability to get accurate information about what happens in the state’s prisons was a repeated complaint from legislators during Tuesday’s hearing. State Rep. Gregg Johnson, D-East Moline, worked for 32 years in the Department of Corrections before he became a lawmaker. He said was concerned that he could not get clear answers to his questions.</p><p>During the hearing, lawyers for incarcerated people referenced the case of Jason Stephens, who was at the center of <a class="Link" href="https://www.themarshallproject.org/2026/07/24/prison-fires-joliet-illinois-mental-health" target="_blank" ><u>the news organizations’ coverage of the dysfunction at the Joliet Treatment Center</u></a>. In 2024, Stephens repeatedly complained the prison was failing to treat his sickle cell disease, causing him extreme pain. He threatened to harm himself until they gave him help. Then on July 27, 2024 Stephens set a fire in his cell.</p><p>Joliet guards left him locked in the smoke-filled cell for around 30 minutes, according to surveillance video reviewed by The Marshall Project. Then, when the fire department put him in an ambulance to go to the hospital, correctional officers would not open the gate for almost 28 more minutes because they were waiting on paperwork and guards to accompany the ambulance. Stephens died two weeks later.</p><p>Representatives for the Illinois Department of Corrections told lawmakers at the hearing that they were limited in what information they could share due to pending litigation. Stephens’ estate is suing the department over his death.</p><p>Antholt said the officers who were working the night Stephens set the fire that killed him were part of a larger, harmful system.</p><p>“Jason Stephens died because he was so desperate to get the help that he needed, that he did the one thing he thought would give the people holding him in that cell no choice but to help him,” Antholt said. “He was wrong.”</p><p>Lawmakers also held a second hearing Tuesday about creating an office to provide independent oversight of Illinois’ prison system. And state Sen. Rachel Ventura, a Democrat whose district includes Joliet, recently filed a resolution in the legislature calling for an independent inspection of fire safety issues at the Joliet Treatment Center.</p>

entries.title: Illinois Holocaust Museum and Education Center in Skokie after 15-month renovation
entries.summary: <p>During a recent walkthrough of the newly renovated Illinois Holocaust Museum and Education Center, a docent told CEO Bernard Cherkasov that the place feels like it has “neshama,” the Hebrew word for “soul” or “spirit.”</p><p>“I don't think I could have asked for a more meaningful response because that is what we were hoping to create,” said Cherkasov during a press preview of the Skokie museum, 9603 Woods Dr., Tuesday.</p><p>After 15 months of construction and more than $10 million in public and private funds and donations, the Skokie museum reopens to the public on Wednesday. Most of the remodeling was done to improve “visitor experience,” Cherkasov said. Updates include accessible bathrooms on each floor, a new welcome center and lobby, a reflection gallery, several newly acquired objects and documents, wider walkways and the new 240-seat Lillian and entries.title: Review: ‘Heroes of the Fourth Turning’ at A Red Orchid Theatre
entries.summary: <p>I often joke with friends about how significantly our world shifted in 2020. Our lives essentially split into a pre- and post-COVID-19 existence, and everything that happened in the before-times feels like it occurred in a completely different lifetime.</p><p>That’s dramatic. But it’s the result of a once-in-a-lifetime global pandemic fused with a nationwide social uprising. Because of these world-halting events, things that happened in 2019 feel ancient.</p><p>These are my thoughts as I squirmed in my seat during the Chicago premiere of Will Arbery’s “Heroes of the Fourth Turning.” The play, which was a Pulitzer Prize finalist, is a talk-heavy, intermissionless, two-hour drama about four friends who reunite in the small town of their Catholic liberal arts college.</p><p>The quartet arrives with intent to celebrate a former mentor and professor who has been named the new president of the institution. But as they catch up on the happenings in each other's lives, secrets are revealed, and ideologies unspool.</p><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="2.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-title"> “Heroes of the Fourth Turning” </div> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f10000" name="module-f10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>When</b>: Through Dec. 6<br><b>Where</b>: A Red Orchid Theatre, 1531 N Wells St.<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://aredorchidtheatre.org/shows/heroes-of-the-fourth-turning/" target="_blank" ><u>Tickets</u></a> from $50; run time is 2 hours with no intermission.</div> </div><p>And all of this takes place on a rural ranch in Wyoming in 2017, during Donald Trump’s first term as President of the United States.</p><p>The play premiered off-Broadway in 2019, so the multitude of Steve Bannon references make sense considering when the script was likely written. Watching the production now, the same week Democrats demolished Trump-backed Republicans in the midterms, not only make the production feel dated, but unfairly comical. It’s impossible to watch these conservative characters without an air of snark as they question such weighty issues as abortion and trans rights, all the while treating the culture wars as an actual impending blood-drawing Civil War. The audience knows what will actually unfold. A lot.</p><p>None of that negates the earnestness in which these fine actors approach this work. Directed by ensemble member Dado, this very much feels like A Red Orchid production. It’s dark, humorous, surreal and thematically challenging, all of which I’ve come to expect and appreciate from this company.</p><p>I am, however, left with the lingering question: Why stage this show now?</p><p>The cast, which includes a riveting performance by Beck Nolan, a talented young actor who audiences may recognize from a role in the Emmy-award winning Apple TV show “Widow’s Bay,” and Chicago theater fans will recognize from his stellar performance in Definition Theatre’s “Keerah” earlier this year, brought apt sincerity to this staging. Nolan portrays Kevin, a curious and neurotic young man who questions both his own faith and the connection between Catholics and political conservatives.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Grofsorean, is a right-wing blogger blinded by the culture wars. She dubs Kevin a “weakling” and seems to truly believe the libs are out to kill the conservatives.</p><p>Some of the most interesting interactions are between Teresa and the chronically ill Emily (Magdalena Dalzell), who once worked a job in Chicago at a clinic where she met pregnant women struggling to decide whether or not to have abortions. Here, the conversation moves from pure politics to humanity itself. Emily is still Catholic, and believes abortion is murder, but meeting these women and understanding their pain — which we learn, she can actually feel — unlocks a compassion that Teresa is unable to grasp.</p><p>Where the production stalls is in the dense dialogue discussing conservative ideals, books and leaders. I do think regional theater, especially in blue cities like Chicago, benefits from showing right-wing characters — and I enjoyed being a fly on the wall for these conversations. But in the years since this play was written, a lot of these particular debates feel settled. The conservative Planned Parenthood takedown doesn’t feel fresh and the conspiracies have long been debunked. This production would work better if I was learning something new, and that is not the fault of anyone on stage.</p><p>The script also feels like it’s missing something. Justin (Nate Santana), a rugged Marine who is ten years older than his classmates, has palpable sexual tension with Emily, yet this passion isn’t explored. Displaying those feelings, and leaving us with no resolution, feels unsatisfying.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f70000" name="image-f70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bd8ad89/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+95/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2F0f%2F58112a214534b34751fc68c710b7%2Fheroes-of-the-fourth-turning-1-photo-by-evan-hanover.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2da55d0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+95/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2F0f%2F58112a214534b34751fc68c710b7%2Fheroes-of-the-fourth-turning-1-photo-by-evan-hanover.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4c1bd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+95/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2F0f%2F58112a214534b34751fc68c710b7%2Fheroes-of-the-fourth-turning-1-photo-by-evan-hanover.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Beck Nolan, Ensemble Member Kirsten Fitzgerald, Nate Santana, Magdalena Dalzell and Isa Grofsorean in A Red Orchid Theatre’s Chicago premiere of Heroes of the Fourth Turning. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4c1bd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+95/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2F0f%2F58112a214534b34751fc68c710b7%2Fheroes-of-the-fourth-turning-1-photo-by-evan-hanover.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/490ce5b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+95/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2F0f%2F58112a214534b34751fc68c710b7%2Fheroes-of-the-fourth-turning-1-photo-by-evan-hanover.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b4c1bd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1800x1010+0+95/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F82%2F0f%2F58112a214534b34751fc68c710b7%2Fheroes-of-the-fourth-turning-1-photo-by-evan-hanover.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The cast, consisting of (from left) Beck Nolan, Kirsten Fitzgerald, Nate Santana, Magdalena Dalzell and Isa Grofsorean, brought apt sincerity to this staging.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Evan Hanover</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The characters themselves have no arcs. Each former student leaves the production in the same place he or she enters without learning anything new or evolving in any significant way. When ensemble member Kirsten Fitzgerald enters the stage as Gina, a former professor and mentor whom the students have gathered to celebrate, she’s a force, as usual. She challenges the students, especially Teresa, with whom she harbors a deep disappointment. But after she storms in and reminds the youngsters she lived through political events they only read about, she just … leaves. And we get no real resolution.</p><p>This production has strong acting, an impressive rural backyard set by Grant Sabin, and compelling scenes that offer insight into conservative ideology. But it feels dated and suffers tremendously from a lack of dramatic tension, which leads to it feeling like two uninterrupted hours of characters talking to each other.</p><p>I think experiencing this play in 2019 would have been illuminating. But seeing it now, it seems to have missed its mark.</p>

entries.summary: <p>In her 1991 TV special “<a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/DYI9rfb6Rmc?si=qsoOSPa4LvjSEnNs" target="_blank" ><u>Going Home to Gospel</u></a>,” Patti LaBelle’s soprano voice fills the sanctuary of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/03/13/chicago-black-church-history-quinn-chapel-ame-slavery-abolitionism-jim-crow-south" target="_blank" ><u>Quinn Chapel AME Church</u></a> as she celebrates a long list of Chicago legends.</p><p>She performs a rousing rendition of “Who’s on the Lord’s Side” with an exuberant Ricky Dillard, who directs his New Generation Chorale. She trades lines with renowned songstress <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/eight-forty-eight/2010/10/14/a-tribute-albertina-walker-queen-of-gospel" target="_blank" ><u>Albertina Walker</u></a> during “I Can Go to God in Prayer.” And she nearly tears up while reciting Gwendolyn Brooks’ poem “Infirm.”</p><p>“So much history is here where I’m standing,” LaBelle says in the special of the now-182-year-old South Side venue — the oldest Black church in Chicago and a stop on the Underground Railroad.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Patti LaBelle in concert</h3><br><b>When:</b> 7 p.m. Nov. 13<br><b>Where:</b> Hard Rock Casino Northern Indiana, 5400 W. 29th Ave., Gary<br><b>Tickets</b>: From $77.35<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="http://casino.hardrock.com/northern-indiana" target="_blank" >casino.hardrock.com/northern-indiana</a><br><br><b>When:</b> 7:30 p.m. Nov. 14<br><b>Where:</b> Genesee Theatre, 203 N. Genesee St., Waukegan<br><b>Tickets:</b> From $97.20<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="http://geneseetheatre.com" target="_blank" >geneseetheatre.com</a></div> </div><p>That gospel tribute is still a core performance memory for LaBelle 25 years later, as she returns to the area to play two shows at Hard Rock Casino Northern Indiana on Friday, and Genesee Theatre in Waukegan on Saturday. Her visits to the Windy City have included performances at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2025/05/31/chaka-khan-patti-labelle-gladys-knight-stephanie-mills-united-center-queens-tour-review" target="_blank" ><u>United Center</u></a> and Arie Crown Theater, book signings at the Unabridged Bookstore, and an appearance at Marshall Field’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Er3LJfBQLz8" target="_blank" ><u>Glamorama</u></a> fashion event.</p><p>But filming the WTTW gospel special in Chicago, considered the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/09/22/overlooked-chicago-gospel-trio-gay-sisters-book" >birthplace of modern gospel</a>, was especially meaningful for LaBelle, now 82. Though she is known for her R&B catalog, her roots are in the church.</p><p>“It was one of the most beautiful moments of my life doing that gospel show,” she said. “I wish I could do it again.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-db0000" name="image-db0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8568e5b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1542x865+0+81/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F50%2F54cd081849ec9210669ee73c7725%2Fpatti-01.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/683bf47/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1542x865+0+81/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F50%2F54cd081849ec9210669ee73c7725%2Fpatti-01.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1e91a36/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1542x865+0+81/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F50%2F54cd081849ec9210669ee73c7725%2Fpatti-01.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Patti LaBelle (second from left) with the Barrett Sisters. The singers appeared on the 1991 WTTW-TV special “Going Home to Gospel.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Paying homage to Chicago’s gospel greats </h3><p>LaBelle doesn’t quite remember how she got involved with the program, but she told the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/1991/03/03/gospel-gala-celebrates-the-music-and-its-artists/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Tribune</u></a> at the time that she wanted to use her popularity to help introduce new audiences to gospel.</p><p>Along with Dillard and Walker, the lineup featured other local performers and speakers, such as Calvin Bridges, Rev. Clay Evans, the Sue Conway Victory Singers, the Chicago Praise Chorale, 14-year-old Deleon Richards and the Barrett Sisters, whom LaBelle praised for their “wonderful harmonies.” The Mighty Clouds of Joy and Edwin Hawkins were also on the bill.</p><p>“So many singers come from Chicago,” LaBelle said. “There’s just so much talent.”</p><p>During the broadcast, LaBelle also delivered history lessons about gospel pioneers and Chicago natives Thomas A. Dorsey and Mahalia Jackson. She impressed with multiple outfit changes and her vocal chops. She closed the show with her dynamic version of “He Cares for You.”</p><p>“I just love that song, and I felt so joyful doing that performance,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> When asked to list her favorite things about Chicago, she mentioned the food (“I love the pizza”) and former President Barack Obama (“He’s such a brilliant man”).</p><p>But she was especially entries.title: From Irish pub to Chicago blues hub: What happened to Biddy Mulligan’s?
entries.summary: <p>In Rogers Park, a block from the lake, weeds are growing in front of a shuttered Irish pub. A sign above the door reads Mulligan’s Cafe, but a marquee above that identifies this closed business by another name: Biddy Mulligan’s. This unassuming storefront was once a hot spot for blues fans on Chicago’s North Side in the 1970s and 1980s.</p><p>During the Great Migration, African Americans moved north to escape Jim Crow-era racism. They brought the blues with them and settled mostly on the South and West sides of Chicago. What started in the Mississippi Delta with a single performer evolved to a more electric sound in the city and was dubbed the “Chicago style” with a full band.</p><p>There were other North Side blues clubs during this era, but how did Biddy Mulligan’s become so iconic? And what happened to the place? The simple answer is a changing neighborhood, shifts in musical tastes and an aging genre. However, to the musicians and regulars of Biddy Mulligan’s, there’s more to this club’s story.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure The storefront has sat vacant for years.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Richard Cotovsky</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Biddy’s foray into the blues</b></h3><p>In the 1970s, places like Theresa’s Lounge and Peppers were legendary clubs in the Bronzeville neighborhood, where the blues was thriving. Greats like Bobby Rush and Otis Clay would perform regularly at these places. Meanwhile, on the North Side, a piano player named Bob Reidy started performing at Biddy Mulligan's with his band. He invited the South and West Side legends to join him and fill out the bill. Biddy’s, located near Northwestern University and Loyola University in Rogers Park, exposed a new and younger audience to the likes of Buddy Guy and Junior Wells.</p><p>The club hit its stride in the late 1970s, when bluegrass banjo player Chip Covington bought the bar. He expanded the work Reidy had begun, and Biddy’s became a North Side hub for the blues. Covington had a deep appreciation for the folk tradition in the genre, and he saw that in the musicians he hired.</p><p>“ I didn’t buy talent because it would fill the room,” he said. “I bought talent because it was authentic.”</p><p>The musical standard at Biddy Mulligan’s was high and competition was fierce. Billy Branch, renowned harmonica player, got his start supporting Willie Dixon. He felt the warmth and accepting nature of Biddy’s, but he also felt the weight.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Dick Shurman, a blues historian, theorized the once “powerful, visceral music… was too old-fashioned and probably understated for the modern audiences.”</p><p>Miller and his wife, Colleen, diversified the acts they brought into Biddy Mulligan’s to keep up with audience preferences. They booked Blues Traveler, who was up and coming at the time. The iconic jam band Phish had their first Chicago gig at Biddy Mulligan’s. There was mixed success but the blues — the primary appeal — was changing.</p><p>Miller sold the club two years later. The next owners tried to adapt to the changing neighborhood and audience by turning the club into a college party scene. But that didn’t work out, and the club closed down.</p><p>Chip Covington had moved back to the U.S. and settled in nearby Evanston with his family. He hated seeing the club sit vacant. He had memories of watching Otis Clay and Otis Rush perform onstage. He met his wife there. So he bought the club back for emotional reasons.</p><p>“I didn’t even really have the money. I went into debt,” he said. “The alderman was very nice. Everybody was very nice who wanted to bring Biddy Mulligan’s back, but it just didn't work.”</p><p>A year later in 1995, Covington closed Biddy Mulligan’s doors for good.</p><p>“ That was about 20 class="Figure-credit"><p>Martin Feldmann</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>What’s next for the blues?</b></h3><p>The closing of Biddy’s is not a unique story in the blues scene. Other storied clubs around Chicago have had to shutter over the years. But there’s still an appetite for the music.</p><p>Billy Branch has devoted a lot of his career to his “Blues in Schools” program across the country and the world. Last year, he did a residency in schools on the West Side of Chicago. He’s eager to shout out the newcomers to the genre.</p><p>“Harrell Davenport goes by the name of Young Rell,” he said. “He’s a walking encyclopedia of knowledge. He knows more about blues history than me and all my friends combined.”</p><p>Branch is also watching King Fish out of Mississippi, Southern Avenue out of Memphis and D.K. Harrell out of Louisiana.</p><p>You can still catch live blues in Chicago.
